| [LIT-002](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-002.md) v2 | Nested Hierarchical Dirichlet Processes | Paisley et al. (2012), [ARXIV-1210.6738](https://arxiv.org/abs/1210.6738). The nHDP gives each document its own DP over the children of every node of a shared global nCRP tree (G_i^(d) ~ DP(βG_i)), plus a per-node stop/continue switch U_{d,i} ~ Beta(γ1, γ2). Each word then takes its own path, and β → 0 recovers the single-path nCRP. The paper fits this with SVI plus a greedy per-document subtree selection. On small corpora the variational nHDP beats variational nCRP on all three datasets and Gibbs nCRP on two of three (PNAS −6.304 vs −6.496/−6.574 held-out log-likelihood). On 1.8M NYT and 2.7M Wikipedia documents it tops stochastic HDP and LDA-50/150/250 by roughly 0.08 and 0.11 nats (read off Figs. 2, 7), using ≈12 and ≈8 topics per document. | Active — read in full 2026-09-25 (NOTE-023); the reference construction of the nHDP and a compact worked example of conjugate-exponential SVI for a tree-structured nonparametric model. Two things about it: the global update equations (23, 26–27) as printed contradict the paper's own §4.1.2 derivation, and the large-scale results never compare against the nCRP. |
| [LIT-013](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-013.md) v2 | Nonparametric Bayesian Topic Modelling with the Hierarchical Pitman-Yor Processes | Lim et al. (2016), [ARXIV-1609.06783](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.06783). The paper collapses every Pitman–Yor node to customer and table counts (Eq. 16, following Chen et al. 2011), which turns any HPYP topic model's posterior into a product of per-node factors, and it samples topics and counts jointly by decrement/propose/increment. The HPYP half of its Twitter-Network Topic Model uses this sampler; the network half is fit by a separate MH step. On one 240,517-tweet, 150-author corpus (T6) the TNTM reaches test perplexity 505.01 ± 7.8, against 664.25 ± 17.76 for a nonparametric ATM and 840.03 ± 15.7 for HDP-LDA, and network log-likelihood −500.63 against −557.86 for the random-function network model alone (Table 4). Removing the power-law discounts barely changes perplexity (508.64) but costs network likelihood (−560.28; Table 5). | Active — read in full 2026-09-25 (NOTE-008); worth reading as a clear, self-contained tutorial on the table-count (Chen et al. 2011) collapsed blocked Gibbs sampler for hierarchical PYPs with discrete and mixture bases. The TNTM experiments are thin: one corpus, clustering baselines copied from another paper, and assertion-level claims about kernels and labels. Cite it for the sampler exposition, not for the empirical superiority of nonparametric models. |
| [LIT-035](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-035.md) v2 | The ergodicity solution of the cooperation puzzle | Peters et al. (2022), DOI-10.1098/rsta.2020.0425. If N entities' resources follow GBM (drift μ, volatility σ, independent noise), then pooling and sharing equally every step leaves the drift at μ, cuts the volatility to σ/√N (Eq. 3.9), and raises each member's time-average growth rate from μ − σ²/2 to μ − σ²/(2N) (Eq. 4.1). The premium is (σ²/2)(1 − 1/N) (Eq. 4.2). With pairwise correlation ρ the effective volatility is σ√((1 + (N−1)ρ)/N), and the large-N limit is μ − σ²ρ/2 (Eqs. 5.12–5.13). | Active — read in full 2026-09-25 ([NOTE-059](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-059.md)); worth reading as the clearest short derivation of the risk-pooling (geometric-mean) advantage of sharing under multiplicative noise. The mathematics is correct and self-contained. The framing claim, that this "solves" the cooperation puzzle and makes cooperation the default, rests on the model's zero-cost, no-cheating assumptions, and the paper's own citations (McCloskey, Winterhalder, Uitdehaag, Kennedy et al.) show the core result was already known. |
| [LIT-038](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-038.md) v2 | The Relativity of Causal Knowledge | D'Acunto et al. (2025), [ARXIV-2503.11718](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.11718). The paper defines SCMs as functors I → Prob and interventions as natural transformations (which requires invertible mixing functions). It encodes each non-intervened SCM as the convex space Δ(V, Ω) of all probability measures on its endogenous space, and puts these spaces on a graph as stalks of a network sheaf and cosheaf. The restriction maps are interventionally consistent α-abstractions and the extension maps are unspecified affine maps. "Relative causal knowledge" is the image of alternating restriction and extension along a path (Def. 11). The two substantive-looking theorems are either unsound or vacuous. Theorem 1 (every convex combination of a model's interventional measures is a soft-interventional measure of it) rests on a proof step that is false. Theorems 2 and 3 hold for any pushforward map, so interventional consistency does no work in them. There are no results about the sheaf. | Rejected — read in full 2026-09-25 (NOTE-050); Not worth a reader's time as a source of results. Its one non-trivial theorem is unsound as proved and false in general, its encoding theorem is vacuous, and §4 contains definitions only. A reader wanting category-theoretic causal abstraction should go to Rischel's thesis or Beckers–Halpern. A reader wanting sheaves on networks should go to Curry or Hansen–Ghrist. |
| [LIT-044](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-044.md) v2 | The Epic Story of Maximum Likelihood | Stigler (2007), [ARXIV-0804.2996](https://arxiv.org/abs/0804.2996). Stigler gives a history of maximum likelihood from Lagrange (1769) to Le Cam (1953). Fisher gave three optimality arguments. The 1922 one rests on the false belief that ML estimates are always sufficient. The 1925 "ANOVA" one derives the information inequality V ≥ 1/I(θ) from Var X = E Var(X\|T) + Var E(X\|T), treating approximate normality as exact. The third, sent privately to Hotelling in 1930, holds for multinomial models and smooth degree-0-homogeneous estimators, and was published only in disguise in 1935. Stigler's verdict is that the Neyman–Scott growing-parameter example (Wald 1938, published 1948) is the practically important failure. He calls Hodges's 1951 superefficiency example "an ingenious but minor technical achievement", because the superefficiency set has Lebesgue measure zero (Le Cam 1953). | Active — read in full 2026-09-25 (NOTE-074); an authoritative, archive-based history by the leading historian of statistics, and worth reading for exactly which ML optimality claims were proved, under what conditions, and which counterexamples matter. It is a history, not a technical reference: for modern conditions it points to Bahadur (1964), Le Cam (1953, 1990), van der Vaart (1998) and Cox (2006). |
| [LIT-048](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-048.md) v2 | Transfer Entropy as a Log-likelihood Ratio | Barnett et al. (2012), [ARXIV-1205.6339](https://arxiv.org/abs/1205.6339). For a parametric Markov model f(x_t \| x^k_t, y^k_t; θ) of X, the likelihood-ratio estimator T̂ = −(1/(n−k)) log Λ for the null "no dependence on Y's past" converges almost surely to the transfer entropy T_{Y→X} (Theorem 1a). Under the null, 2(n−k)T̂ is asymptotically χ²(d), with d the difference in parameter counts (Theorem 1b). For finite-state chains the ordinary plug-in estimator is exactly this estimator, with d = (a−1)a^k(b^k−1). For a linear Gaussian VAR, T̂ is half the Granger-causality statistic. | Active — read in full 2026-09-25 (NOTE-053); a short, correct letter and the standard citation for reading transfer entropy as a log-likelihood ratio. The consistency proof is informal, and the χ² results are cited to Wald (1943) rather than proved, but the identity itself is exact and still the one to cite. |
| [LIT-050](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-050.md) v2 | Mean-Field-Type Game Theory with Rosenblatt Noise | Tembine et al. (2025), [ARXIV-2506.08025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08025). The paper's control and game results use linear state feedback, and they depend on the Rosenblatt noise only through its covariance, which is exactly fBM's with the same H. They are therefore identical to the fBM results. The ergodic LQ gain (Thm 4), K̂ = −[b₁ + √(b₁² + 4H(1−H)b₂²q/r)]/(2b₂(1−H)), is correct and reduces to the Brownian LQR gain at H = ½. But the paper's headline "suboptimality of noise approximation" (§VI-A, repeated for the variance-aware control, zero-sum, non-zero-sum and MFTG settings) holds only against surrogates with a different covariance; against fBM with the same H it is false. The ML claim that Rosenblatt "super-diffusion transformers" "significantly enhance the performance of generative machine intelligence models" (§XIV-C) has no model, training, dataset or experiment behind it anywhere in the paper. | Rejected — read in full 2026-09-25 (NOTE-068); not worth a reader's time. The control-theoretic results are earlier papers' (its refs [43]–[46]) restated. Its central new claim, that Gaussian and fBM surrogates give suboptimal control, is false for fBM with matching H, since the costs depend only on covariance. Its empirical sections are unsourced vignettes: numbers without references, "Rosenblatt shape" fits without any fitting procedure, and data from the first author's own startups. Its ML claim is an assertion with no model or experiment. A reader wanting Rosenblatt-noise LQ control should go to Čoupek–Duncan–Maslowski–Pasik-Duncan (CDC 2018, ref [43]) and Čoupek–Duncan–Pasik-Duncan (SPA 2022, ref [27]). |
| [LIT-058](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-058.md) v3 | Mutual Information and Minimum Mean-square Error in Gaussian Channels | Guo et al. (2004), [arXiv:cs/0412108](https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0412108). Let Y = √snr·X + N with N ~ N(0,1) independent of X, and let X have any distribution with E X² < ∞. Then d/dsnr I(X; √snr X + N) = ½·mmse(X \| √snr X + N) in nats, equivalently I(snr) = ½∫₀^snr mmse(γ) dγ (Thm 1, Eq. 47). The vector form is d/dsnr I(X; √snr HX + N) = ½·E‖HX − H·E[X\|Y]‖² (Thm 2). In continuous time, the same identity combined with Duncan's I = (snr/2)·cmmse gives cmmse(snr) = (1/snr)∫₀^snr mmse(γ) dγ (Thm 8). | Active — read in full 2026-09-25 (NOTE-086); the founding statement and proof of the I-MMSE identity. It is fully proved (five proofs, with the interchange of limits justified in App. IV) and it remains the reference. Read §II-C for the incremental-channel proof and §V-B for the one place it fails (feedback). |
| [LIT-064](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-064.md) v3 | Talagrand Meets Talagrand: Upper and Lower Bounds on Expected Soft Maxima of Gaussian Processes with Finite Index Sets | Chu et al. (2025), [ARXIV-2502.06709](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.06709). Take a centered Gaussian process on a finite set T with max variance σ² and minimum separation a. The expected softmax-weighted average g(β) = E[Σ_t X_t e^{βX_t}/Z] satisfies g(β) ≤ √(2σ²·E D(ν_β‖ν₀)) for every β (Thm 1, D = KL from uniform). For β ≥ β*, g(β) ≥ c·a·√(E D(ν_β‖ν₀)), with c the Sudakov constant (1/17 via Marcus–Rosen) (Thm 2). For i.i.d. N(0,σ²) logits there is an exact identity, g(β) = βσ²(1 − E‖ν_β‖²₂) (Lemma 2). The quenched free energy is bounded above by √(2σ²·E D_{1/2}(ν_β‖ν₀)), with an i.i.d. lower bound of (cσ/2)√(E D_{1/2}) (Thms 4–5). | Superseded — by ANTH-LIT-726; moved to the Anthology of the SOTA as ANTH-LIT-726 on 2026-09-26, at the owner's request, with its Read NOTE; nothing is held in both records (ADR-001) |

| [LIT-077](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-077.md) v2 | What is quantum in quantum randomness? | Grangier et al. (2018), [ARXIV-1804.04807](https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.04807). The paper argues informally, with no equations anywhere in it, that an "elementary" system with a fixed finite number N of exclusive modalities, placed in contexts that can change, must behave unpredictably when the context changes: a return to C1 after C2 cannot be certain, or there would be N² > N joint modalities (p. 4). It asserts that adding one condition, that the context can change continuously, makes the N×N modality-transition matrix unistochastic, i.e. Born-rule, but defers that proof to refs [14, 15] (p. 5). The anti-reductionist conclusion follows from Postulate 0, which declares contexts non-contextual by definition, not from an argument against decoherence. | Active — read in full 2026-09-25 (NOTE-044); a short, equation-free position paper whose one argument of its own is an informal N = 2 reductio; read it for the position, and read the derivation it cites — Auffèves & Grangier, Sci. Rep. 2017 (arXiv 1610.06164) and arXiv 1801.01398, neither held here — for the result. |
| [LIT-085](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-085.md) v3 | The No-U-Turn Sampler: Adaptively Setting Path Lengths in Hamiltonian Monte Carlo | Hoffman et al. (2011), [ARXIV-1111.4246](https://arxiv.org/abs/1111.4246). NUTS removes HMC's step-count L. It doubles a leapfrog trajectory forwards and backwards in random directions until some balanced subtree satisfies (θ⁺−θ⁻)·r⁻ < 0 or (θ⁺−θ⁻)·r⁺ < 0. It keeps detailed balance by slice sampling and by excluding states that could not have regenerated the tree. With ε set by a dual-averaging scheme (γ = 0.05, t₀ = 10, κ = 0.75, target δ ≈ 0.6), it matched the best hand-tuned HMC in ESS per gradient on two logistic-regression posteriors. It beat that HMC by about 3× on a 250-D Gaussian and on a 3001-D stochastic-volatility model (§4.4). | Active — read in full 2026-09-25 (NOTE-081); This is the source of the default sampler in Stan, PyMC and NumPyro, and it is worth reading for its derivation. The algorithm as run today, with multinomial rather than slice selection and adapted mass matrices, is documented elsewhere. A reader who wants current practice should read this paper together with that later account. |
| [LIT-086](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-086.md) v2 | The Stochastic-Quantum Correspondence | Barandes (2023), [ARXIV-2302.10778](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.10778). Take any N×N stochastic transition matrix Γ(t←0) on a configuration space. Writing it entrywise as Γ_ij = \|Θ_ij\|² = tr(Θ†P_iΘP_j) (Eq. 15) is always possible, and the paper calls it the stochastic-quantum dictionary. Choosing Θ unitary (by Stinespring dilation to ≤N³ configurations, §3.4) makes Γ unistochastic. The Born rule in the configuration basis (Eq. 23), the Schrödinger equation (Eq. 35, with H ≡ iħ(∂U/∂t)U†) and interference (Eq. 43, the gap between Γ(t←0) and \|U(t←t′)\|²\|U(t′←0)\|²) then follow by definition or short algebra. The Born rule for non-diagonal observables (Eq. 78) is derived by reading a measuring device's configuration, given a composite unitary that produces Eq. (73). | Active — read in full 2026-09-25 (NOTE-080); the clearest single statement of the indivisible-stochastic-process reading of quantum theory, and its measurement model (§4) is worth reading. Discount its "new result" labels: the dictionary is an identity, the Schrödinger equation is the definition of H, and unitarity is a representational choice the paper's own gauge footnote does not preserve. |
